e-5266.knowledge_point: Identifying Properties of an Elliptic Paraboloid
e-5266.problem: Find the vertex and the axis of symmetry of the elliptic paraboloid $z= 4x^2 + 8(y + 2)^2.$
e-5266.worked_solution:
The general equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $z$-axis with vertex at a point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ is 

$$
z - z_0 = \dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2}.
$$

To find the vertex, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-0 & =4{x}^{2}+8(y+2)^{2} \\ z-0 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{1/4}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{1/8} \\ z-0 & =\frac{(x-0)^{2}}{1/4}+\frac{(y-(-2))^{2}}{1/8}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $z$-axis that has its vertex at $(0,-2,0).$  Since it is oriented along the $z$-axis, we conclude that its axis of symmetry is parallel to the $z$-axis.

The axis of symmetry should pass through the vertex of the paraboloid. Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry can be written as an intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=0 \\ y=-2\end{aligned}
$$

e-5269.knowledge_point: Identifying Properties of a Hyperbolic Paraboloid
e-5269.problem: Find the saddle point of the hyperbolic paraboloid $z+1=\dfrac{(x-1)^2}{4} - (y-2) ^2.$
e-5269.worked_solution:
The general equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ is given by

$$
z - z_0 = \dfrac{(x-x_0)^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{(y-y_0)^2}{b^2}.
$$

To find the saddle point, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z+1 & =\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{4}-(y-2)^{2} \\ z-(-1) & =\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{4}-(y-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $(1,2,-1).$

e-6087.problem:
The projection of the intersection between the hyperbolic paraboloid 

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{4} - \dfrac{(y+5) ^2}{3} = z-1
$$

and the plane $x=2$  onto the $yz$-plane is a parabola. Find the vertex of this parabola.
e-6087.worked_solution:
To find the intersection of the paraboloid and the plane $x=2,$ we substitute $x=2$ into the equation of the paraboloid and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-\frac{(y+5)^{2}}{3} & =z-1 \\ \frac{{2}^{2}}{4}-\frac{(y+5)^{2}}{3} & =z-1 \\ 1-\frac{(y+5)^{2}}{3} & =z-1 \\ z & =-\frac{1}{3}(y+5)^{2}+2\end{aligned}
$$

Projecting this onto the $yz$-plane, we get the equation of a parabola that has its vertex at $(-5,2).$

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Consider the elliptic paraboloid $z=\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{2}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4}.$ Which of the following gives its axis of symmetry, written as an intersection of two planes?
after.worked_solution:
First, we write our equation as 

$$
z-0=\frac{(x-(-1))^{2}}{2}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4}.
$$

This gives us the equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $z$-axis that has its vertex at $(-1,2,0).$
 Since it is oriented along the $z$-axis, we conclude that its axis of symmetry is parallel to the $z$-axis.

The axis of symmetry should pass through the vertex of the paraboloid. Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry can be written as an intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-1 \\ y=2\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Consider the elliptic paraboloid $z=\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{2}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4}.$ Which of the following gives its axis of symmetry, written as an intersection of two planes?
content.worked_solution:
First, we write our equation as 

$$
z-0=\frac{(x-(-1))^{2}}{2}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4}.
$$

This gives us the equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $z$-axis that has its vertex at $(-1,2,0).$
 Since it is oriented along the $z$-axis, we conclude that its axis of symmetry is parallel to the $z$-axis.

The axis of symmetry should pass through the vertex of the paraboloid. Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry can be written as an intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-1 \\ y=2\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Consider the elliptic paraboloid $y+1=\frac{(x+4)^{2}}{5}+\frac{(z-2)^{2}}{3}.$ Which of the following gives its axis of symmetry, written as an intersection of two planes?
after.worked_solution:
First, we write our equation as 

$$
y-(-1)=\frac{(x-(-4))^{2}}{5}+\frac{(z-2)^{2}}{3}.
$$

This gives us the equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $y$-axis that has its vertex at $(-4,-1,2).$
 Since it is oriented along the $y$-axis, we conclude that its axis of symmetry is parallel to the $y$-axis.

The axis of symmetry should pass through the vertex of the paraboloid. Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry can be written as an intersection of two planes:

$$

content.problem: Consider the elliptic paraboloid $y+1=\frac{(x+4)^{2}}{5}+\frac{(z-2)^{2}}{3}.$ Which of the following gives its axis of symmetry, written as an intersection of two planes?
content.worked_solution:
First, we write our equation as 

$$
y-(-1)=\frac{(x-(-4))^{2}}{5}+\frac{(z-2)^{2}}{3}.
$$

This gives us the equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $y$-axis that has its vertex at $(-4,-1,2).$
 Since it is oriented along the $y$-axis, we conclude that its axis of symmetry is parallel to the $y$-axis.

The axis of symmetry should pass through the vertex of the paraboloid. Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry can be written as an intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-4 \\ z=2\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Find the vertex of the elliptic paraboloid $3z+6=3(x-3)^{2}+(y+2)^{2}.$
after.worked_solution:
The general equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $z$-axis with vertex at a point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is 

$$
z-{z}_{0}=\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}.
$$

To find the vertex, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3z+6 & =3(x-3)^{2}+(y+2)^{2} \\ 3(z+2) & =3(x-3)^{2}+(y+2)^{2} \\ z+2 & =(x-3)^{2}+\frac{1}{3}(y+2)^{2} \\ z-(-2) & =(x-3)^{2}+\frac{(y-(-2))^{2}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of an elliptic paraboloid that has its vertex at $(3,-2,-2).$

EXPLANATION

The general equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the z-axis with vertex at a point (x0,y0,z0) is z−z0=(x−x0)2a2+(y−y0)2b2.

To find the vertex, we rewrite our equation as follows:

3z+6=3(x−3)2+(y+2)23(z+2)=3(x−3)2+(y+2)2z+2=(x−3)2+13(y+2)2z−(−2)=(x−3)2+(y−(−2))23

This gives us the equation of an elliptic paraboloid that has its vertex at (3,−2,−2).

content.knowledge_point: Identifying Properties of an Elliptic Paraboloid
content.problem: Find the vertex of the elliptic paraboloid $3z+6=3(x-3)^{2}+(y+2)^{2}.$
content.worked_solution:
The general equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $z$-axis with vertex at a point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is 

$$
z-{z}_{0}=\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}.
$$

To find the vertex, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3z+6 & =3(x-3)^{2}+(y+2)^{2} \\ 3(z+2) & =3(x-3)^{2}+(y+2)^{2} \\ z+2 & =(x-3)^{2}+\frac{1}{3}(y+2)^{2} \\ z-(-2) & =(x-3)^{2}+\frac{(y-(-2))^{2}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of an elliptic paraboloid that has its vertex at $(3,-2,-2).$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Consider the elliptic paraboloid $x=\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{2}+\frac{(z+1)^{2}}{6}.$ Which of the following gives its axis of symmetry, written as an intersection of two planes?
after.worked_solution:
First, we write our equation as 

$$
x-0=\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{2}+\frac{(z-(-1))^{2}}{6}.
$$

This gives us the equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $x$-axis that has its vertex at $(0,3,-1).$
 Since it is oriented along the $x$-axis, we conclude that its axis of symmetry is parallel to the $x$-axis.

The axis of symmetry should pass through the vertex of the paraboloid. Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry can be written as an intersection of two planes:

$$

The axis of symmetry should pass through the vertex of the paraboloid. Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry can be written as an intersection of two planes:

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms the vertex is (0,3,-1) and the axis is parallel to the x-axis. Therefore y=3 and z=-1, matching option b. The deliberately incorrect submission selected a.

content.knowledge_point: Identifying Properties of an Elliptic Paraboloid
content.problem: Consider the elliptic paraboloid $x=\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{2}+\frac{(z+1)^{2}}{6}.$ Which of the following gives its axis of symmetry, written as an intersection of two planes?
content.worked_solution:
First, we write our equation as 

$$
x-0=\frac{(y-3)^{2}}{2}+\frac{(z-(-1))^{2}}{6}.
$$

This gives us the equation of an elliptic paraboloid oriented along the $x$-axis that has its vertex at $(0,3,-1).$
 Since it is oriented along the $x$-axis, we conclude that its axis of symmetry is parallel to the $x$-axis.

The axis of symmetry should pass through the vertex of the paraboloid. Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry can be written as an intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=3 \\ z=-1\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Given the elliptic paraboloid $z+13=\frac{(x-5)^{2}}{5}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{2}$, find its intercepts with the $y$-axis.
after.worked_solution:
To find the $y$-intercepts of the paraboloid, we substitute $x=0$ and $z=0$ into the equation of the paraboloid and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}0+13 & =\frac{(0-5)^{2}}{5}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{2} \\ 13 & =\frac{25}{5}+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{2} \\ 13 & =5+\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{2} \\ \frac{(y+1)^{2}}{2} & =8 \\ (y+1)^{2} & =16 \\ y+1 & =\pm 4\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the solutions $y=3,-5.$ 

Therefore, the intercepts with the $y$-axis are $(0,-5,0)$ and $(0,3,0).$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Find the saddle point of the hyperbolic paraboloid $z-3=\frac{(x+2)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{4}.$
after.worked_solution:
The general equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is 

$$
z-{z}_{0}=\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}.
$$

To find the saddle point, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-3 & =\frac{(x+2)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{4} \\ z-3 & =\frac{(x-(-2))^{2}}{2}-\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The general equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at (x0,y0,z0) is z−z0=(x−x0)2a2−(y−y0)2b2.

To find the saddle point, we rewrite our equation as follows:

z−3=(x+2)22−(y−4)24z−3=(x−(−2))22−(y−4)24

This gives us the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at (−2,4,3).

content.problem: Find the saddle point of the hyperbolic paraboloid $z-3=\frac{(x+2)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{4}.$
content.worked_solution:
The general equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is 

$$
z-{z}_{0}=\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}.
$$

To find the saddle point, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-3 & =\frac{(x+2)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{4} \\ z-3 & =\frac{(x-(-2))^{2}}{2}-\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $(-2,4,3).$

Question 7

Find the saddle point of the hyperbolic paraboloid z+2=(x+5)23−(y−2)22.

a
(−5,2,−2)
b
(−5,−2,2)
c
(5,−2,−2)
d
(−2,5,−2)
e
(5,−2,2)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The general equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at (x0,y0,z0) is z−z0=(x−x0)2a2−(y−y0)2b2.

To find the saddle point, we rewrite our equation as follows:

z+2=(x+5)23−(y−2)22z−(−2)=(x−(−5))23−(y−2)22

This gives us the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at (−5,2,−2).

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms x₀=-5, y₀=2, and z₀=-2, so the saddle point is (-5,2,-2), option a. The deliberately incorrect submission selected e.

content.knowledge_point: Identifying Properties of a Hyperbolic Paraboloid
content.problem: Find the saddle point of the hyperbolic paraboloid $z+2=\frac{(x+5)^{2}}{3}-\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{2}.$
content.worked_solution:
The general equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is 

$$
z-{z}_{0}=\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}.
$$

To find the saddle point, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z+2 & =\frac{(x+5)^{2}}{3}-\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{2} \\ z-(-2) & =\frac{(x-(-5))^{2}}{3}-\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $(-5,2,-2).$

Question 8
?

Given the hyperbolic paraboloid (x+3)2−2(y−3)2=z−2, find its intercepts with the x-axis.

a
(−7,0,0) and (−1,0,0)
b
(−7,0,0) only
c
(−1,0,0) and (7,0,0)
d
(−7,0,0) and (1,0,0)
e
(1,0,0)
Submit

decision.explanation: On the x-axis, y=0 and z=0. Thus (x+3)^2-18=-2, so (x+3)^2=16 and x=-7 or x=1. The intercepts are (-7,0,0) and (1,0,0).

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: Given the hyperbolic paraboloid $(x+3)^{2}-2(y-3)^{2}=z-2$, find its intercepts with the $x$-axis.
after.worked_solution:
To find the $x$-intercepts of the paraboloid, we substitute $y=0$ and $z=0$ in the equation of the paraboloid:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2}-2(0-3)^{2} & =0-2 \\ (x+3)^{2}-18 & =-2 \\ (x+3)^{2} & =16 \\ x+3 & =\pm 4 \\ x & =-3\pm 4\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the solutions $x=-7$ and $x=1.$

Therefore, the intercepts with the $x$-axis are $(-7,0,0)$ and $(1,0,0).$

Question 8
?

Given the hyperbolic paraboloid (x+3)2−2(y−3)2=z−2, find its intercepts with the x-axis.

a
(−7,0,0) and (−1,0,0)
b
(−7,0,0) only
c
(−1,0,0) and (7,0,0)
d
(−7,0,0) and (1,0,0)
e
(1,0,0)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the x-intercepts of the paraboloid, we substitute y=0 and z=0 in the equation of the paraboloid:

(x+3)2−2(0−3)2=0−2(x+3)2−18=−2(x+3)2=16x+3=±4x=−3±4

This gives the solutions x=−7 and x=1.

Therefore, the intercepts with the x-axis are (−7,0,0) and (1,0,0).

content.knowledge_point: Identifying Properties of a Hyperbolic Paraboloid
content.problem: Given the hyperbolic paraboloid $(x+3)^{2}-2(y-3)^{2}=z-2$, find its intercepts with the $x$-axis.
content.worked_solution:
To find the $x$-intercepts of the paraboloid, we substitute $y=0$ and $z=0$ in the equation of the paraboloid:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2}-2(0-3)^{2} & =0-2 \\ (x+3)^{2}-18 & =-2 \\ (x+3)^{2} & =16 \\ x+3 & =\pm 4 \\ x & =-3\pm 4\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the solutions $x=-7$ and $x=1.$

Therefore, the intercepts with the $x$-axis are $(-7,0,0)$ and $(1,0,0).$

decision.explanation: The squared terms are centered at x=1 and y=-4. At that point both vanish, giving z=5, so the saddle point is (1,-4,5).

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Find the saddle point of the hyperbolic paraboloid $z-5=5(x-1)^{2}-3(y+4)^{2}.$
after.worked_solution:
The general equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is 

$$
z-{z}_{0}=\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}.
$$

To find the saddle point, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-5 & =5(x-1)^{2}-3(y+4)^{2} \\ z-5 & =\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{1/5}-\frac{(y+4)^{2}}{1/3} \\ z-5 & =\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{1/5}-\frac{(y-(-4))^{2}}{1/3}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $(1,-4,5).$

content.problem: Find the saddle point of the hyperbolic paraboloid $z-5=5(x-1)^{2}-3(y+4)^{2}.$
content.worked_solution:
The general equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is 

$$
z-{z}_{0}=\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}.
$$

To find the saddle point, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-5 & =5(x-1)^{2}-3(y+4)^{2} \\ z-5 & =\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{1/5}-\frac{(y+4)^{2}}{1/3} \\ z-5 & =\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{1/5}-\frac{(y-(-4))^{2}}{1/3}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $(1,-4,5).$

decision.explanation: On the x-axis, y=0 and z=0. Substitution gives 2(x-5)^2-3=5, so (x-5)^2=4. Hence x=3 or x=7, yielding (3,0,0) and (7,0,0).

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Given the hyperbolic paraboloid $2(x-5)^{2}-3(y-1)^{2}=z+5$, find its intercepts with the $x$-axis.
after.worked_solution:
To find the $x$-intercepts of the paraboloid, we substitute $y=0$ and $z=0$ in the equation of the paraboloid:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(x-5)^{2}-3(0-1)^{2} & =0+5 \\ 2(x-5)^{2}-3 & =5 \\ 2(x-5)^{2} & =8 \\ (x-5)^{2} & =4 \\ x-5 & =\pm 2 \\ x & =5\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10

Given the hyperbolic paraboloid 2(x−5)2−3(y−1)2=z+5, find its intercepts with the x-axis.

a
(3,0,0) and (7,0,0)
b
(−2,0,0) and (2,0,0)
c
(7,0,0) only
d
(−3,0,0) and (2,0,0)
e
(5,0,0) only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the x-intercepts of the paraboloid, we substitute y=0 and z=0 in the equation of the paraboloid:

2(x−5)2−3(0−1)2=0+52(x−5)2−3=52(x−5)2=8(x−5)2=4x−5=±2x=5±2

This gives the solutions x=3 and x=7.

Therefore, the intercepts with the x-axis are (3,0,0) and (7,0,0).

content.knowledge_point: Identifying Properties of a Hyperbolic Paraboloid
content.problem: Given the hyperbolic paraboloid $2(x-5)^{2}-3(y-1)^{2}=z+5$, find its intercepts with the $x$-axis.
content.worked_solution:
To find the $x$-intercepts of the paraboloid, we substitute $y=0$ and $z=0$ in the equation of the paraboloid:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(x-5)^{2}-3(0-1)^{2} & =0+5 \\ 2(x-5)^{2}-3 & =5 \\ 2(x-5)^{2} & =8 \\ (x-5)^{2} & =4 \\ x-5 & =\pm 2 \\ x & =5\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the solutions $x=3$ and $x=7.$

Therefore, the intercepts with the $x$-axis are $(3,0,0)$ and $(7,0,0).$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: What is the trace in the $yz$-plane of the elliptic paraboloid $z+1=\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{3}.$
after.worked_solution:
To find the trace in the $yz$-plane, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}z+1 & =\frac{(0-2)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{3} \\ z+1 & =\frac{4}{4}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{3} \\ z+1 & =1+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{3} \\ z & =\frac{1}{3}(y-1)^{2}\end{aligned}

Question 11

What is the trace in the yz-plane of the elliptic paraboloid z+1=(x−2)24+(y−1)23.

a
Two parallel lines: y=(z±3)
b
A parabola: z=3(y−1)2
c
A parabola: z=13(y−1)2
d
Two intersecting lines: y=±(x−1)
e
A hyperbola: x2−3(y−1)2=1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the trace in the yz-plane, we substitute x=0 into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

z+1=(0−2)24+(y−1)23z+1=44+(y−1)23z+1=1+(y−1)23z=13(y−1)2

This gives us the equation of the parabola in yz-plane.

content.problem: What is the trace in the $yz$-plane of the elliptic paraboloid $z+1=\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{3}.$
content.worked_solution:
To find the trace in the $yz$-plane, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}z+1 & =\frac{(0-2)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{3} \\ z+1 & =\frac{4}{4}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{3} \\ z+1 & =1+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{3} \\ z & =\frac{1}{3}(y-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

This gives us the equation of the parabola in $yz$-plane.

content.problem: What is the trace in the $yz$-plane of the elliptic paraboloid $z=\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{27}.$
content.worked_solution:
To find the trace in the $yz$-plane, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{{0}^{2}}{8}+\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{27} \\ z & =\frac{1}{27}(y-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

This gives us the equation of the parabola in $yz$-plane.

Question 13
?

The projection of the intersection between the elliptic paraboloid 4(x−5)2+6(y+4)2=z+8 and the plane z=4 onto the xy-plane is an ellipse. What are the lengths of the semi-axes of the ellipse?

a
3 and 2
b
3 and 2
c
3 and 1
d
9 and 4
e
22 and 1
Submit

decision.explanation: Setting z=4 gives 4(x-5)^2+6(y+4)^2=12. Dividing by 12 yields (x-5)^2/3+(y+4)^2/2=1, so the semi-axis lengths are √3 and √2.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
The projection of the intersection between the elliptic paraboloid $4(x-5)^{2}+6(y+4)^{2}=z+8$ and the plane 
$z=4$  onto the $xy$-plane is an ellipse. What are the lengths of the semi-axes of the ellipse?
after.worked_solution:
To find the intersection of the paraboloid and the plane $z=4$, we substitute $z=4$ into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x-5)^{2}+6(y+4)^{2}=z+8 \\ 4(x-5)^{2}+6(y+4)^{2}=4+8 \\ 4(x-5)^{2}+6(y+4)^{2}=12 \\ \frac{(x-5)^{2}}{3}+\frac{(y+4)^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-5)^{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}}+\frac{(y+4)^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of an ellipse with semi-axes of lengths $\sqrt{3}$ and $\sqrt{2}.$

Question 13
?

The projection of the intersection between the elliptic paraboloid 4(x−5)2+6(y+4)2=z+8 and the plane z=4 onto the xy-plane is an ellipse. What are the lengths of the semi-axes of the ellipse?

a
3 and 2
b
3 and 2
c
3 and 1
d
9 and 4
e
22 and 1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the intersection of the paraboloid and the plane z=4, we substitute z=4 into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

4(x−5)2+6(y+4)2=z+84(x−5)2+6(y+4)2=4+84(x−5)2+6(y+4)2=12(x−5)23+(y+4)22=1(x−5)2(3)2+(y+4)2(2)2=1

This gives us the equation of an ellipse with semi-axes of lengths 3 and 2.

content.problem:
The projection of the intersection between the elliptic paraboloid $4(x-5)^{2}+6(y+4)^{2}=z+8$ and the plane 
$z=4$  onto the $xy$-plane is an ellipse. What are the lengths of the semi-axes of the ellipse?
content.worked_solution:
To find the intersection of the paraboloid and the plane $z=4$, we substitute $z=4$ into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x-5)^{2}+6(y+4)^{2}=z+8 \\ 4(x-5)^{2}+6(y+4)^{2}=4+8 \\ 4(x-5)^{2}+6(y+4)^{2}=12 \\ \frac{(x-5)^{2}}{3}+\frac{(y+4)^{2}}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-5)^{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}}+\frac{(y+4)^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of an ellipse with semi-axes of lengths $\sqrt{3}$ and $\sqrt{2}.$

Question 14

The projection of the intersection between the hyperbolic paraboloid (x+1)24−y29=z+2 and the plane y=3 onto the xz-plane is a parabola. What is the vertex of this parabola?

a
(1,3) in the xz-plane
b
(1,−3) in the xz-plane
c
(0,0) in the xz-plane
d
(−1,3) in the xz-plane
e
(−1,−3) in the xz-plane
Submit

decision.explanation: Substituting y=3 gives (x+1)^2/4-1=z+2, hence z=(x+1)^2/4-3. The vertex in the xz-plane is (-1,-3).

after.name: Question 14
after.problem:
The projection of the intersection between the hyperbolic paraboloid $\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}=z+2$ and the plane 
$y=3$  onto the $xz$-plane is a parabola. What is the vertex of this parabola?
after.worked_solution:
To find the intersection of the paraboloid and the plane $y=3$, we substitute $y=3$ into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =z+2 \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{{3}^{2}}{9} & =z+2 \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}-1 & =z+2 \\ z+3 & =\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4} \\ z & =\frac{1}{4}(x+1)^{2}-3\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a parabola in the $xz$-plane that has its vertex at $(-1,-3).$

Question 14
?

The projection of the intersection between the hyperbolic paraboloid (x+1)24−y29=z+2 and the plane y=3 onto the xz-plane is a parabola. What is the vertex of this parabola?

a
(1,3) in the xz-plane
b
(1,−3) in the xz-plane
c
(0,0) in the xz-plane
d
(−1,3) in the xz-plane
e
(−1,−3) in the xz-plane
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find the intersection of the paraboloid and the plane y=3, we substitute y=3 into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

(x+1)24−y29=z+2(x+1)24−329=z+2(x+1)24−1=z+2z+3=(x+1)24z=14(x+1)2−3

This gives us the equation of a parabola in the xz-plane that has its vertex at (−1,−3).

verification.explanation: The revealed solution gives z=(x+1)^2/4-3, whose vertex is (-1,-3) in the xz-plane. This confirms option e; the deliberately incorrect submission selected a.

content.problem:
The projection of the intersection between the hyperbolic paraboloid $\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}=z+2$ and the plane 
$y=3$  onto the $xz$-plane is a parabola. What is the vertex of this parabola?
content.worked_solution:
To find the intersection of the paraboloid and the plane $y=3$, we substitute $y=3$ into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =z+2 \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}-\frac{{3}^{2}}{9} & =z+2 \\ \frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4}-1 & =z+2 \\ z+3 & =\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4} \\ z & =\frac{1}{4}(x+1)^{2}-3\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a parabola in the $xz$-plane that has its vertex at $(-1,-3).$

decision.explanation: Setting z=2 gives 5(x+2)^2+3(y+3)^2=2. The squared terms are centered at x=-2 and y=-3, so the ellipse has center (-2,-3).

after.name: Question 15
after.problem: The projection of the intersection between the elliptic paraboloid $5(x+2)^{2}+3(y+3)^{2}=z$ and the plane $z=2$  onto the $xy$-plane is an ellipse. Find the center of this ellipse.
after.worked_solution:
To find the intersection of the paraboloid and the plane $z=2$, we substitute $z=2$ into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}5(x+2)^{2}+3(y+3)^{2} & =z \\ 5(x+2)^{2}+3(y+3)^{2} & =2 \\ \frac{(x+2)^{2}}{2/5}+\frac{(y+3)^{2}}{2/3} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of an ellipse in the $xy$-plane that has its center at $(-2,-3).$

The projection of the intersection between the elliptic paraboloid 5(x+2)2+3(y+3)2=z and the plane z=2 onto the xy-plane is an ellipse. Find the center of this ellipse.

a
(2,−3) in the xy-plane
b
(2,3) in the xy-plane
c
(0,0) in the xy-plane
d
(−2,−3) in the xy-plane
e
(−2,3) in the xy-plane
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the intersection of the paraboloid and the plane z=2, we substitute z=2 into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

5(x+2)2+3(y+3)2=z5(x+2)2+3(y+3)2=2(x+2)22/5+(y+3)22/3=1

This gives us the equation of an ellipse in the xy-plane that has its center at (−2,−3).

content.problem: The projection of the intersection between the elliptic paraboloid $5(x+2)^{2}+3(y+3)^{2}=z$ and the plane $z=2$  onto the $xy$-plane is an ellipse. Find the center of this ellipse.
content.worked_solution:
To find the intersection of the paraboloid and the plane $z=2$, we substitute $z=2$ into the equation of the paraboloid, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}5(x+2)^{2}+3(y+3)^{2} & =z \\ 5(x+2)^{2}+3(y+3)^{2} & =2 \\ \frac{(x+2)^{2}}{2/5}+\frac{(y+3)^{2}}{2/3} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of an ellipse in the $xy$-plane that has its center at $(-2,-3).$
